question: The Circular Economy Act, due for adoption in 2026, aims to enhance the EU’s economic security, resilience, competitiveness and decarbonisation efforts. The Steel and Metals Action Plan recognises that the metals industry represented 8.1 % of total EU greenhouse gas emissions in 2022.

Scrap steel from end-of-life ships represents an opportunity to put both initiatives into action while supporting the EU’s ship dismantling sector, as well as its know-how and workers, which is currently facing unfair competition from non-EU countries.

A recent study from Shipbreaking Platform, Sandbag and the University of Tuscia illustrates the significant potential of scrap steel from end-of-life ships in the decarbonisation efforts of the EU’s steel industry. Around 12 000 of the vessels owned by EU and European Free Trade Association countries are expected to become eligible for scrapping by 2035, generating about 12 Mt of scrap steel per year.
Mandatory recycled-content requirements for steel could be a good way to stimulate a market for ship scrap. Given the strategic importance of this sector, how is the Commission: 1.
planning to ensure that EU-owned ships are not exported and that their materials are retained within the EU?
addressing the practice of re-flagging ships shortly before demolition?
considering the rapid introduction of strong circularity incentives, such as a ship recycling licence, in line with its study on the matter?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.2.2026) The Ship Recycling Regulation (SRR)1 aims to reduce the adverse effects on human health and the environment of ship recycling. It is based on international rules2 and applies only to EU-flagged ships.

These ships must be recycled in yards that are in the European list of ship recycling facilities and that comply with strict safety and environmental requirements, irrespective of their location (in the EU or not). Furthermore, for any ships that become waste in the EU, the Waste Shipment Regulation3 imposes an export ban to non-Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development countries.

The evaluation of the SRR of February 20254 concludes that the effectiveness of the SRR has been significantly undermined by re-flagging, as highlighted by the Honourable Members. A potential financial incentive such as a ship recycling licence to prevent SRR circumvention, would need to be assessed further as part of an impact assessment in the context of a future possible revision process of the SRR.

The Commission considers the first priority is to see how the Hong Kong Convention5, which entered into force in June 2025, can be improved towards stricter global standards. Re-flagging is also a global issue which cannot be solved through the SRR only. In this respect, the Commission published in January 2026 a study on the use of the ‘open registers’ (often related to ‘flags of convenience’)6.
In addition, the Commission continues to monitor the SRR implementation, collaborating with enforcement authorities and stakeholders, with a focus on preventing circumvention.
1 Regulation (EU) No 1257/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 November 2013 on ship
recycling and amending Regulation (EC) No 1013/2006 and Directive 2009/16/EC, OJ L 330, 10.12.2013, pp. 1–20.

2 It is in accordance with relevant Hong Kong Convention provisions and taking into account the relevant guidelines of the International Maritime Organization, the International Labour Organization, the Basel Convention and the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants and of other international guidelines.

3 Regulation (EU) 2024/1157 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 April 2024 on shipments of waste, amending Regulations (EU) No 1257/2013 and (EU) 2020/1056 and repealing Regulation (EC) No 1013/2006, OJ L, 2024/1157, 30.4.2024. 4 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:52025SC0040. 5 https://www.imo.
